bpLabel: Fieldstrip Best Practices guide. No manufacturer manual exists for this model, so we built this from general best practices for this type of firearm. It does not represent manufacturer data. If you obtain the factory manual, follow it over this guide. Never take a firearm further apart than this guide goes unless its maker documents it.
cleanIntro:
No manual from Heritage exists for this model, so this guide works from what is true of every revolver of its kind, and asks you which kind yours is: one whose cylinder swings out to the side, or one loaded through a gate behind the cylinder. The revolver comes apart only as far as its own design allows by hand; the lockwork never comes out.

Listed in Fieldstrip as .38 Special. The chambering marked on the gun itself is the one that counts — not this guide, and not the listing.

steps.title: Ammunition out of the room, muzzle somewhere safe
steps.action: Before you start, put every loose cartridge, loaded magazine and box of ammunition in another room — a cleaning bench with live rounds on it is where unintended discharges happen. Keep the muzzle pointed where a shot would hurt no one, and keep your finger outside the trigger guard the whole time. Wear eye protection whenever you use solvent or work near a spring, and work where the air moves.
steps.prose: A safety, if yours has one, is never a substitute for an empty chamber, and nothing in this guide relies on one.

steps.title: Which revolver is it? Look at the cylinder
steps.action: Look at the frame just behind the cylinder, usually on the right. If there is a small hinged gate there that swings open to show one chamber at a time, yours is a loading-gate revolver. If there is no gate, and a release beside the frame lets the whole cylinder swing out to the side, yours is a swing-out revolver. Follow the steps for yours and skip the others.
steps.prose: ⛔ If you cannot tell, stop here and contact Heritage — never pry at a cylinder to find out.

steps.title: Swing-out: hammer down, cylinder out, rod pushed
steps.action: Only for a swing-out cylinder. With the hammer down and your finger off the trigger, work the cylinder release — it is pushed forward, pulled back or pressed in depending on the design, and you can see which way it is shaped to move — and swing the cylinder out. Point the muzzle up and push the ejector rod firmly to clear every chamber, then let the rod return on its own.

steps.title: Loading gate: one chamber at a time
steps.action: Only for a loading gate. Open the gate. On some revolvers of this kind the hammer must first be drawn back to its loading notch — a light click partway back — before the cylinder will turn; on others the open gate alone frees it. Turn the cylinder by hand until each chamber in turn lines up with the gate, and push each case out with the ejector rod under the barrel.
steps.prose: ⛔ If the cylinder will not turn with the gate open and you do not know whether yours needs the loading notch, stop and contact Heritage. Never force a cylinder to turn.

steps.title: Every chamber, by eye and by finger — twice
steps.action: Look into every chamber and run a fingertip across the rear face of the cylinder. Count them as you go: a chamber you skipped is a chamber you did not check. Then do it all a second time.
steps.prose: ⛔ If a case will not come out, stop: never pry or hammer it — contact Heritage.

steps.title: Swing-out: the open cylinder is the whole strip
steps.action: Only for a swing-out revolver. With the cylinder swung out, everything an owner cleans is within reach, and that is as far as this revolver comes apart. The crane screw, the sideplate and the lockwork behind it are never touched — on a revolver with no published procedure, those are work for Heritage.

steps.title: Loading gate: cylinder out, only if a latch frees the base pin
steps.action: Only for a loading-gate revolver. Look at the front of the frame, under the barrel, at what holds the base pin — the long pin the cylinder turns on. If a spring-loaded button crosses the frame there, press it and draw the base pin forward out of the frame; then, with the gate open — and the hammer at its loading notch if yours has one — roll the cylinder out of the frame to the gate side. If a screw holds the base pin, or you see no button, stop: the cylinder stays in and is cleaned through the gate.
steps.prose: Note which way round the cylinder came out; it goes back the same way.

steps.title: The bore, from the breech end when it is open
steps.action: With a swing-out cylinder open, or a loading-gate cylinder out, the rear of the barrel is exposed: push a brush wet with bore solvent from there through to the muzzle, then dry patches until they come out clean. With a loading-gate cylinder still in, work from the muzzle with a rod guide so the rod never rubs the crown. Finish with a lightly oiled patch for storage, and run a dry patch through before you shoot.
steps.prose: The crown — the edge of the muzzle — is what decides where the shot goes; a rod dragged across it does lasting harm.

steps.title: Each chamber on its own
steps.action: A bore brush is the wrong size for a chamber. Use a chamber brush or a patch on a jag, one chamber at a time — through the gate if the cylinder is still in. Pay attention to the chamber mouths: lead and copper build a ring there that makes cases stick and extraction stiff.

steps.title: Cylinder face, forcing cone and the ejector star
steps.action: The front face of the cylinder and the rear face of the barrel take the worst of the blast; clean the grey ring off both with a small brush and a little solvent. On a swing-out revolver, push the ejector rod so the star lifts, clean under it, and let it seat: packed powder there stops the cylinder closing. Then a thin film of oil in the bore and chambers for storage and a trace on the crane or the base pin — and none into the lockwork from the outside.

steps.title: Look for the things that mean stop
steps.action: Hold the barrel up to the light and look through it: you want a clean, unbroken bore with no obstruction, no bulge and no dark ring. Look over the forcing cone, the cylinder and the frame for cracks, a bent ejector rod, and for anything loose or missing. A screw or pin that has worked loose is reported, not tightened — how tight it should be is a question for Heritage.
steps.prose: Any one of these means the gun is not fired until Heritage has seen it.

deepAbsentReason: There is no deep clean for the Heritage Roscoe, and this guide will not invent one. No manual from Heritage exists for this model, so nothing about the inside of it can be known from a document. Anything that needs more than this guide goes to Heritage, not onto the bench.

cleaning.name: BORE
tasks: From the breech end when the cylinder is open or out; otherwise from the muzzle with a rod guide
Brush wet with bore solvent, then dry patches until clean
A lightly oiled patch for storage; a dry patch before the next shot

cleaning.name: CHAMBERS
tasks: Each chamber on its own, with a chamber brush or a patch on a jag
The ring at each chamber mouth

cleaning.name: CYLINDER & FRAME
tasks: Cylinder face and the barrel's rear face
Under the ejector star on a swing-out cylinder
A trace of oil on the crane or the base pin
⛔ No oil into the lockwork from the outside

cleaning.name: EXTERIOR
tasks: Wiped with a lightly oiled cloth
No solvent on wood, finishes or optics

cleaning.name: STORAGE
tasks: Stored dry — never shut in a closed case while damp
Looked over for rust at every clean

reassembly: Swing-out: the cylinder swung closed until its latch clicks — it should close without force.
Loading gate, if the cylinder came out: the cylinder rolled back in from the gate side, the base pin slid back in from the front until its latch catches, and the gate closed.
Swing-out, closed: the cylinder is locked and does not spin freely. Loading gate, gate open: the cylinder turns and clicks into line with each chamber in turn.
fncheck: Every chamber empty. A swing-out cylinder opens, closes and latches without force. A loading-gate cylinder turns with the gate open and clicks into line with each chamber, and the gate stays shut when closed. This check never asks you to cock the hammer or pull the trigger — whether a revolver of unknown design may be dry-fired is a question for Heritage.
